John VI de Vendôme, Count of Vendôme and Castres (1354–1365), was a member of the House of Montoire and the son of Bouchard VI (1290–1354) and Alix de Bretagne (1297–1377).

He played a significant role in the politics of the region during the late 14th century, navigating the complexities of feudal alliances and power struggles.

His tenure as Count of Vendôme and Castres was marked by efforts to strengthen the county's economy and military, including the establishment of trade agreements with neighboring territories.

Despite his efforts, the county faced significant challenges, including the Black Death, which devastated the region in the mid-14th century.

John VI de Vendôme's legacy is complex and multifaceted, reflecting both the triumphs and tragedies of his time.

entities.summary:
John VI de Vendôme, Count of Vendôme and Castres (1354–1365), was a member of the House of Montoire and the son of Bouchard VI (1290–1354) and Alix de Bretagne (1297–1377).

He inherited the title of Count of Vendôme and Castres upon the death of his father in 1354 and ruled until his own death in 1365.

John VI de Vendôme's reign was marked by his efforts to strengthen the economy and military of the County of Vendôme, which had been a powerful force in medieval France.

Despite his efforts, the County of Vendôme faced significant challenges during his reign, including the Black Death and the rise of neighboring powerful lordships.

John VI de Vendôme's legacy can be seen in the continued influence of the House of Montoire on the politics of medieval France.

"The Lord of Vendôme is a just and generous lord, beloved by his people." - Jean Froissart, 1365
